subject: Chem
title: Acids, Periodic Table & metals
sub: Acids, bases and salts, the Periodic Table, metals, reactivity, corrosion and extraction
strategyIntro: Cambridge IGCSE Co-ordinated Sciences tests chemistry alongside biology and physics: a multiple-choice paper (40 questions, 45 min), a theory paper of structured questions, and a practical or alternative-to-practical paper. Your school test may be shorter, but it will be marked the same way.

strategy.title: Multiple choice
points: About a minute per question. If one is taking longer, mark it and move on.
Cross out options you know are wrong first. Two often look similar: read every word.
Never leave one blank. A wrong answer loses nothing.

strategy.title: Structured questions
points: Marks go to keywords. Write the textbook term: “effervescence” or “fizzing”, not “it reacts”.
The marks in brackets tell you how many separate points to make.
Equations: check every atom balances, and add state symbols when the question asks.

strategy.title: Questions on experiments
points: Results tables: units go in the column headings, not next to each number.
Colour changes need both colours: “blue to white”, not just “white”.
Know the control variables and one safety precaution for each experiment.

strategy.title: Easy marks people lose
points: Saying ionic bonds “share” electrons. Ionic = transfer; covalent = share.
Writing “chlorine” when you mean the chloride ion, or “clear” when you mean “colourless”.
Calculations without units, or without the working shown.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
quizIntro: Answer in Paper 1 style: about a minute each, eliminating wrong options first. Read the explanation after every answer, even when you get it right.
flashIntro: These are close to Cambridge’s own wording. Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords. Cards marked (Extended) are Supplement content.

flashcards.back: Has a pH below 7. Turns blue litmus red and methyl orange red.
A base neutralises an acid (e.g. metal oxides and hydroxides). An alkali is a soluble base: pH above 7, turns red litmus blue and thymolphthalein blue.
Universal indicator: pH 1–6 acidic (red, orange, yellow), pH 7 neutral (green), pH 8–14 alkaline (blue, purple). Lower pH = more acidic.
Acid + base → salt + water. (Extended) Ionic equation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Salt + hydrogen. E.g. zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen.
Salt + water + carbon dioxide. You see fizzing (effervescence).
Hydrochloric acid → chlorides; sulfuric acid → sulfates; nitric acid → nitrates.
Metal oxides are basic. Non-metal oxides (e.g. CO₂, SO₂) are acidic. (Extended) Amphoteric oxides, such as aluminium oxide and zinc oxide, react with both acids and bases.

flashcards.front: Making a soluble salt from an insoluble base
flashcards.back: Add excess base to warm acid, filter off the excess, heat the filtrate to the crystallisation point, leave to cool, then filter and dry the crystals.
Acids are proton (H⁺) donors; bases are proton acceptors.
A strong acid is completely dissociated into ions in water (e.g. hydrochloric acid). A weak acid is only partially dissociated (e.g. ethanoic acid).

flashcards.front: How the Periodic Table is arranged
flashcards.back: In order of increasing proton number. Groups are the vertical columns; periods are the horizontal rows.

flashcards.front: Why elements in a group are similar
flashcards.back: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, so they have similar chemical properties.
Elements change from metals on the left to non-metals on the right.
Lithium, sodium, potassium. Soft, low-density metals. React with water to form an alkaline hydroxide solution and hydrogen. Reactivity increases and melting point decreases down the group.

flashcards.front: Group I with water: what you see
flashcards.back: Lithium fizzes steadily. Sodium melts into a ball and moves around on the surface. Potassium reacts more violently and the hydrogen burns with a lilac flame.
Diatomic non-metals. Chlorine: pale yellow-green gas; bromine: red-brown liquid; iodine: grey-black solid. Reactivity decreases down the group; density increases.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its halide. Chlorine + potassium bromide → potassium chloride + bromine (solution turns orange).
Metals with high densities and high melting points. They form coloured compounds and they (and their compounds) act as catalysts. (Extended) They have variable oxidation numbers.
Unreactive, monatomic gases because they have a full outer shell. Helium: balloons (low density). Argon: filling lamps (unreactive).
Rubidium is below potassium, so it reacts even more violently with water. Astatine is below iodine, so it is a dark solid and less reactive than iodine.
Good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable, ductile, shiny, and most have high melting and boiling points.
A mixture of a metal with other elements. Brass = copper and zinc. Stainless steel = iron with chromium, nickel and carbon.
Atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other so easily.
Aluminium: aircraft (low density, strong) and food containers (resists corrosion). Copper: electrical wiring (good conductor, ductile). Stainless steel: cutlery (resists rusting).
Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold.
K, Na, Ca react with cold water. Mg reacts very slowly with cold water but quickly with steam. Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to give hydrogen; copper, silver and gold do not.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. Zinc + copper(II) sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper.
Iron reacts with water and oxygen to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Both water and oxygen are needed.
Barrier methods (paint, grease, plastic coating) keep out water and oxygen. Galvanising coats iron with zinc, which is more reactive and corrodes first (sacrificial protection).
Raw materials: haematite (iron(III) oxide), coke (carbon), limestone, hot air. Coke burns to CO₂; CO₂ + C → 2CO; carbon monoxide reduces the ore: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.
It decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with sand (silicon dioxide) impurities to form slag (calcium silicate): CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃.
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so it is extracted by electrolysis of aluminium oxide (from bauxite) dissolved in molten cryolite.

quiz.q: A solution has a pH of 13. How is it best described?
quiz.why: pH above 7 is alkaline, and 13 is near the top of the scale, so strongly alkaline. Universal indicator would be purple.

quiz.q: Which gas is made when zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
quiz.why: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Carbon dioxide comes from carbonates.

quiz.q: Which salt is made when copper(II) oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
quiz.why: Sulfuric acid makes sulfates. Sulfides contain no oxygen and are not made this way.

quiz.q: What colour is thymolphthalein in an alkaline solution?
quiz.why: Thymolphthalein is colourless in acid and blue in alkali. Methyl orange is the one that is red in acid and yellow in alkali.

quiz.q: When making copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and sulfuric acid, why is the copper(II) oxide added in excess?
options: To make the solution strongly alkaline
To make sure all the acid is used up
quiz.why: Excess base guarantees no acid is left in the salt solution. The unreacted solid is then removed by filtering.

quiz.q: (Extended) Which of these is a weak acid?
quiz.why: Ethanoic acid only partly dissociates into ions in water. The other three are strong acids.

quiz.q: Which trend is correct going down Group I?
quiz.why: Group I metals get more reactive and have lower melting points down the group. Atoms get larger as shells are added.

quiz.q: Chlorine water is added to colourless potassium iodide solution. What is seen?
options: The solution turns brown as iodine is displaced
quiz.why: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine, which colours the solution brown.

quiz.q: Why is argon used inside filament lamps?
options: It glows when it gets hot
quiz.why: Argon has a full outer shell and does not react with the hot filament, so the filament does not burn away.

quiz.q: Which property do transition elements have that Group I metals do not?
quiz.why: Group I compounds are usually white. Coloured compounds and catalytic activity are typical of transition elements.

quiz.q: Element X has the electronic configuration 2,8,7. Where is it in the Periodic Table?
quiz.why: Seven outer electrons → Group VII. Three occupied shells → period 3. This is chlorine.

quiz.q: Which metal is the most reactive?
quiz.why: In the reactivity series magnesium is above zinc, iron and copper.

quiz.q: An iron nail is placed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. What is seen?
options: Nothing, because iron is less reactive than copper
A pink-brown coating of copper forms on the nail
quiz.why: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper. The blue colour fades as iron(II) sulfate forms.

quiz.q: Why is copper used for electrical wiring?
options: It is a good conductor of electricity and ductile
quiz.why: Wires must conduct well and be drawn into thin strands (ductile). Copper is not magnetic and is unreactive.

quiz.q: Which conditions are needed for iron to rust?
quiz.why: Rusting needs both water and oxygen. Remove either one (e.g. with a barrier) and it stops.

quiz.q: Why does a coating of zinc protect iron even when the coating is scratched?
options: Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron
Zinc is less reactive than iron
Zinc turns the iron into an alloy
quiz.why: This is sacrificial protection: the more reactive zinc loses electrons and corrodes first, so the iron does not rust.

quiz.q: In the blast furnace, which substance reduces iron(III) oxide to iron?
quiz.why: Carbon monoxide takes oxygen away from iron(III) oxide and is oxidised to carbon dioxide.

examIntro: Theory-paper style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme and give yourself one mark per point you made clearly. One point per mark is the rule.

exam.q: Write a word equation for the reaction between sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid, and name this type of reaction.
points: Sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water
Neutralisation

exam.q: Calcium carbonate is added to dilute nitric acid. State two observations and write the word equation.
points: Fizzing / effervescence / bubbles
Solid disappears / dissolves
Calcium carbonate + nitric acid → calcium nitrate + …
… + water + carbon dioxide
exam.note: One mark for naming the salt, one for the other two products.

exam.q: Describe how you would make pure, dry crystals of copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.
points: Warm the dilute sulfuric acid
Add copper(II) oxide a little at a time, stirring
Until it is in excess / black solid remains undissolved
Filter to remove the excess copper(II) oxide
Heat the filtrate to evaporate some water, to the crystallisation point
Leave to cool so crystals form
Filter off the crystals and dry them between filter paper

exam.q: A small piece of sodium is added to a trough of water. State two observations.
points: Floats
Melts into a ball
Moves around on the surface
Fizzes / bubbles
Gets smaller and disappears

exam.q: Chlorine is bubbled into colourless potassium bromide solution. Describe what is seen, write a word equation, and explain the reaction.
points: Solution turns orange (yellow-orange)
Chlorine + potassium bromide → potassium chloride + bromine
Chlorine is more reactive than bromine
So chlorine displaces bromine from its compound

exam.q: Describe the trend in reactivity of the Group I metals and use it to predict how rubidium reacts with water.
points: Reactivity increases down the group
Rubidium reacts more violently than potassium (explosively)
Forms rubidium hydroxide
And hydrogen gas
The solution formed is alkaline (high pH)
(Extended) The outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily

exam.q: Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis and not by heating its oxide with carbon.
points: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon
So carbon cannot remove oxygen from (reduce) aluminium oxide

exam.q: Describe and explain two different ways of preventing a steel bicycle from rusting.
points: Paint the frame / oil or grease the chain
This forms a barrier that keeps out water and oxygen
Galvanise: coat with zinc
Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron, even when scratched
exam.note: Two marks for each method: the method, then how it works.

exam.q: Describe how iron is extracted from haematite in the blast furnace. Include equations.
points: Haematite, coke and limestone are added at the top; hot air is blown in at the bottom
Coke (carbon) burns in the air, releasing heat: C + O₂ → CO₂
Carbon dioxide reacts with more coke to form carbon monoxide: CO₂ + C → 2CO
Carbon monoxide reduces iron(III) oxide to iron
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
Molten iron runs to the bottom and is tapped off
Limestone removes impurities (sand) as slag
